Each one contains all three meanings,
as extensively discussed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) and so forth.
Second, the censure of the five desires:
These refer to visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"Restrain the six sense faculties as one would tether a dog, a deer, a fish, a snake, a monkey, and a bird."
Dogs delight in villages;
deer delight in mountain marshes;
fish delight in ponds and pools.
The snake delights in dwelling in its hole;
the monkey delights in the deep forest;
the bird delights in relying upon the void.
The six sense organs delighting in the six sense objects cannot be subdued by those of ordinary people with shallow wisdom and weak resolve;
they can only be overcome by great wisdom, a firm mind, and right mindfulness.
Only then can they be subdued.
This was a general exhortation regarding the six sense faculties;
now I shall address them individually.
The eye craves forms;
forms possess substantial images like a village,
and the eye is like a dog.
The ear craves sounds.
Sounds have no substantial form, being like an empty marsh;
the ear is like a deer.
The nose craves fragrances like a fish;
the tongue craves flavors like a snake;
the body clings to tactile sensations like a monkey.
The mind taking dharmas as its object is like a bird.
Now, setting aside the mental faculty, we clarify that while the five sense objects themselves are not desire,
they possess flavors that can give rise to the mind of craving in the practitioner.
Therefore, they are called the five desires.
For example, it is like a potter who, when invited by a patron nearby, cannot apply himself to his work;
the five desires are just like this.
It constantly seeks to draw people into the realms of Māra;
thus, although one possesses the aforementioned conditions, it is difficult for the mind to remain established.
Therefore, it must be rebuked.
As for form (*rūpa*), it refers to the red and white, the long and short, the bright eyes with their graceful glances, the fair neck, the azure eyebrows, the white teeth, and the crimson lips;
and even to the secondary environment (*upabhoga*) consisting of various precious objects in red, yellow, vermilion, and purple.
Delusions disturb the human mind;
as explained in the Chan school,
the harm caused by sensory forms (*rūpa*) is particularly profound.
It causes people to become crazed and intoxicated.
The very root of birth and death truly lies herein.
As a sutra says:
Sentient beings are greedily covetous of wealth and sensual pleasures;
because of this, they fail to attain the Way.
As the *Sūtra on Contemplation* states:
One is driven by form and enslaved by affection,
unable to attain self-mastery.
If one can know the faults and afflictions of form, [one will be liberated].
Thus one will not be deceived.
Having been rebuked in this way, desire for form immediately ceases;
the攀緣 (pān-yuan, object-conditioning) does not arise.
One enters meditative concentration with single-minded focus.
As for "desire for sound," this refers to coquettish and seductive phrases, lewd sounds, and defiling speech.
The sounds of silk strings, flutes, lutes, and pipes, as well as the tinkling of bracelets and pendants,
constitute the desire for sound. As for the desire for fragrance,
it refers to objects that are dense and pervasive, such as the scent of orchids and musk, which are fragrant, intense, and luxuriantly abundant.
As well as the scents of the bodies of men and women and so forth.

Regarding the desire for flavors, this refers to wine, meat, delicacies, fatty and oily foods, sweet, sour, salty, and pungent tastes, clarified butter, fresh blood, and the like. Regarding the desire for touch:
These are what are called garments and superior clothing— namely, cold, heat, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, strength, and softness—
as well as the physical bodies of men and women.
Such are the faults and afflictions of these five desires.
Visible forms are like glowing iron balls; if one grasps them, they burn.
Sounds are like drums smeared with poison; if one hears them, one will surely die.
Fragrances are like the breath of a dead dragon; if one smells them, one falls ill. Tastes are like boiling honey soup; if one tastes them, the tongue is scorched.
Like licking a knife coated with honey, one is wounded;
like touching a sleeping lion, one is bitten upon approaching.
These five desires bring no satiety when obtained.
Their evil intent increases like fire fed with fuel;
from lifetime to lifetime they cause harm more severe than that of enemies or bandits,
constantly plundering one another throughout successive kalpas.
The crushing of body and mind now obstructs meditative stillness and further causes disturbance;
one should deeply recognize the fault of this craving and bring it to rest.
This is the contemplation of the mind that reviles the five desires.
Just as there are immeasurable flavors within form and desire—
namely, permanence and impermanence, self and non-self, purity and impurity, suffering and pleasure, and emptiness—
so too does the ultimate truth exist.
All of these are flavors.
The *Śāstra* states: "The two vehicles, for the sake of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), disparage material phenomena;
therefore, it is not called a *pāramitā*."
When a bodhisattva reviles form, they see the true mark of form;
seeing the true mark of form is precisely seeing the true mark of dhyāna.
Therefore, it is called a pāramitā.
To reach the other shore of form is to see the Middle Way.
To discriminate form is [to fall into extremes].
To see form as conventional is to see the falsity of form;
to see that form is empty is to see the truth of form.
Thus, having reviled form and exhausted the very source and bottom of form,
one accomplishes the samādhi of the three truths and gives rise to the three kinds of wisdom.
The profound censure of form is intended as a skillful means for contemplating the mind;
this is its underlying purpose. Since this is the case regarding the censure of form, [the same applies to the other aggregates].
The other four are likewise.
Regarding the abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*):
these are sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
The general designation "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) is used because these states shroud and entangle the mind,
causing the mental faculty to become darkened; since concentration and wisdom do not arise, they are called hindrances.
The previous condemnation of the five desires refers to the five consciousnesses arising from the five sense organs in response to the five present objects;
the current abandonment of the five hindrances refers to these five consciousnesses transforming and entering the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Chasing after past conditions and speculating about the future regarding the phenomena of the five sensory objects constitutes a great internal obstacle for the mind;
it is like a potter who, being afflicted by illness within his own body, is unable to engage in his craft.
It is likewise in this case:
since the hindrance is already profound,
it is further compounded by abandonment.
It is like pruning a poisonous tree or apprehending a thief; one must not allow it to remain.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"One leaves behind desire and unwholesome dharmas."
"Free from desire" refers to the five objects of sensual desire.
This is as previously stated regarding the censure of unwholesome dharmas.
These are the five hindrances;
they must be abandoned with urgency.
As for these five hindrances:
What are its characteristics?
The hindrance of sensual desire arises from recollecting the five objects of desire experienced in the past,
and from recollecting pure and clean forms that have come into contact with the eye.
One recollects the lovely sounds as if they were faintly present in the ears;
one contemplates the pleasing fragrances which open the gates of the fetters and latent tendencies;
one imagines the delicious flavors as sweet nectar flowing into the mouth.
Craving hundreds of millions of tactile sensations, their hair stands on end and they tremble with agitation;
they greedily desire such coarse and base five sensual pleasures,
and through such mental deliberations and calculations, their minds become intoxicated and deluded.
They lose right mindfulness,
or they secretly employ expedient means,
hoping to obtain it once more.
If one has not yet attained it, one should further investigate;
or when seeking and searching, the mind enters into sensory objects without any intervening thought.
Gross discursive thought obstructs meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
By what means is concentration attained?
This is called the characteristic of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).
The hindrance of ill will consists of recollecting how a certain person has harmed me or my kin,
or has praised my enemies.
Bound by resentment through the nine types of affliction across the three periods of time,
their minds burn with heat and their breath is coarse as anger continues in succession;
they employ a hundred stratagems to seek their prey.
Among the characteristics of desire is malice:
endangering others to secure one’s own safety, indulging in poisonous anger,
and taking pleasure in the full satisfaction of one's passions.
In this way, the fire of hatred burns away all merits;
how then could the branches and groves of meditative concentration grow?
This is the characteristic of the hindrance of hatred.
Regarding the hindrance of sleep (*middha-nīvaraṇa*):
when the mind and spirit are in a state of profound dullness and the six consciousnesses are obstructed by darkness, the four limbs become slack and listless; this is sleep.
Sleep is called an increased mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*).
Like a dark, dense, and heavy mist that comes and covers a person,
it is difficult to guard against.
The five sensory faculties are devoid of consciousness, like those of a dead person;
merely having a few remaining breaths is called "minor death.
If one delights in sleep, then sleep will increase ever more.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If one is hindered by excessive sleep and indolence,
those things not yet attained will remain unattained, and those already attained will be lost."
If one wishes to overcome sleep, doubt, and negligence on the path,
the *Śāstra* says:
"It is like a person who has been bound and is being led away to execution."
How could one possibly sleep at such a time?
It is like standing amidst the white blades on a battlefield,
or dwelling in the same room as a venomous serpent.
At such a time, how could one sleep?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In the middle watch of the night, recite the sūtras to serve as a means of rest."
They vied with one another to seek their way out of the burning house;
a foot-long jade disc is no treasure compared to the competition for even an inch of time.
Now that you cultivate the wondrous Way, how can you indulge in idle sleep?
One must not be deluded regarding this principle and should certainly abandon it. As for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*):
if initial and sustained mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) arise predominantly, they are subsumed under the aforementioned hindrance.
Now, as vitarka and vicāra arise and universally take all phenomena as their objects,
they may momentarily take desire as their object,
or again, they may conceive of hatred and delusion.
Blazing without ceasing, towering without abiding;
now rising, now subsiding, all manner of confusion.
The body wanders aimlessly, and the mouth engages in useless chatter.
This is called restlessness.
When there is restlessness but no remorse, it does not constitute a hindrance;
this is because of that restlessness.
Reflecting within your own mind, you ought to be cautious and restrained;
why do you instead engage in such useless activities?
This is truly a cause for shame.
When sorrow, regret, and vexation bind and entangle the mind within,
they constitute the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
This hindrance covers meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), preventing it from being developed.
Therefore it is said: "Once you have repented, do not grieve further;
you should not dwell constantly on it, nor act upon what should not be done."
To fail to perform what ought to be done—
this is precisely that intention.
This is called the characteristic of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-āvaraṇa*): this is not the doubt that obstructs the principle of seeing the truths;
rather, it is the doubt that obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are three kinds of doubt:
first, doubt regarding oneself;
second, doubt regarding the teacher.
Third, the three types of doubt regarding the Dharma. First, self-doubt:
this refers to doubting one's own body, thinking, "I am of lowly station and certainly not a vessel for the Way. This is doubt concerning the body.
Second, those who doubt the teacher:
"This person's body and speech do not accord with my own inclinations;
how could he possibly possess profound meditation and excellent wisdom?"
One serves them as teachers.
Regarding the three doubts concerning the Dharma:
one wonders whether the Dharma received must necessarily accord with reason.
Third, doubt and hesitation constantly dwell within one's heart;
meditative concentration fails to arise, and even if attained, it is lost forever.
This is the characteristic of the hindrance of doubt.
What is the characteristic of abandonment?
A practitioner constantly examines himself:
"Which illness currently predominates within my mind?"
If one knows a person is ill, one should treat them first.
If the hindrance of craving is heavy, one should employ the contemplation of impurity to discard it.
Why, then, did you previously claim that the five desires are pure and that one is bound by attachment to them?
Now, observing this impure sack of pus, mucus, and saliva, there is nothing in it to rejoice in.
If this covering were removed,
the mind would immediately find peace.
If the hindrance of ill-will is predominant,
one should contemplate loving-kindness to extinguish the fire of hatred;
for this fire can burn away the merit of both worlds.
People do not like to see [such a person].
Now, by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness,
one abandons this evil and regards all people with the thought that they are one's own parents.
Causing all to obtain happiness.
When one contemplates in this way, the mind of anger immediately subsides,
and the mind settles as one enters meditative absorption.
If the hindrance of drowsiness is prevalent,
one should apply oneself with diligent vigor, exerting both body and mind,
and with focused intent, remain vigilant and contemplate the characteristics of phenomena.
Do not, on account of sleep, lose the happiness of both worlds;
you will live and die in vain, with nothing gained at all,
like one who enters a mountain of jewels and returns empty-handed.
This is truly lamentable;
one should skillfully restrain the mind and adeptly ward it off.
As for the hindrance of agitation and distraction:
One should apply the practice of counting the breaths. Why is this?
Because it is exceedingly beneficial.
When returning, one does not realize it for a long time before becoming aware of it.

Now, when counting the breaths, if the counting is not successful, or if one forgets during the process, one should recognize that it has already passed; once one becomes aware of this, one should begin counting again.
When the characteristics of the [meditative] counts are perfected, vitarka and vicāra are subdued;
if one does not treat them, they will shroud one for the rest of one's life.
As for those who harbor the three doubts within their hearts:
He forms this thought:
"I am indeed a blind child of great wealth,
fully endowed with the treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma-body."
The eye of the Path is obscured by afflictions and has not yet opened;
do not bring about your own ruin through doubt.
If you should doubt the teacher...
I am now without wisdom.
The supreme sages and great beings all seek the Dharma and do not take up the person.
[Thus it was that] on the Snowy Mountains, one requested a verse from a ghost.
The Heavenly Emperor bowed to an animal and took it as his teacher.
If you doubt the Dharma,
it is because my eye of Dharma has not yet opened and I have not yet distinguished right from wrong.
It is simply a matter of faith.
The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean; only through faith can one enter it.
Thus, a sutra says:
Although various paths are displayed, their reality is but the One Vehicle.
Do not doubt the various teachings that serve as the means of expression;
simply grasp the true principle that is expressed.
When these three doubts are abandoned,
their five hindrances are likewise discarded. Indeed,
these five hindrances are themselves the afflictions and unwholesome dharmas of birth and death.
The Sūtra says:
"Afflictions are themselves awakening; birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa.
However, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa exist in accordance with the delusion or enlightenment of sentient beings.
Thus, there arises the distinction between the two rivers;
yet in reality, there is no birth-and-death,
and the five hindrances may be abandoned.
The dharma of nirvana can be sought;
this is thus to discard what is not to be discarded,
which is called discarding the five hindrances.
Regarding the four ways of regulating the five matters:
these are regulating clothing, regulating food, regulating the body, regulating the breath, and regulating the mind.
First, regulating sleep:
However, sleep is the nutriment of the eye;
when it is excessive, one becomes drowsy and naturally impaired.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
It is like a person who loves sleep; if they sleep excessively,
their vision will fail when it is deficient,
as was the case with Aniruddha.
Now, by regulating them so they attain their proper state, one causes the mind to settle in contemplative observation, whereby wisdom becomes luminous and pure.
As for internal correspondence: ignorance and afflictions are sleep;
the followers of the Two Vehicles have completely severed these afflictions.
Just as one who sleeps excessively is unbalanced,
ordinary beings who have not severed [afflictions] are like those who do not regulate their sleep;
the Bodhisattva differs from these two extremes.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Not dwelling in a mind of discipline, nor dwelling in a mind of indiscipline—
this is the bodhisattva’s subduing of sleep."
Second, regarding the regulation of food:
eating too much hinders sitting [in meditation],
while eating too little results in a state of emptiness and weakness.
"Eating neither too little nor too much is the mark of balanced eating.
Regarding the contemplative understanding of this,
the Sūtra says:
To discern the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna as one's food:
to lean toward emptiness alone is excessive hunger;
to lean toward the provisional alone is excessive satiety.
The equanimity of the Madhyamaka is the characteristic of balanced diet.
Regarding the three ways of adjusting the body:
when sitting, holding the torso upright is the characteristic of excessive tension.
When sitting, the head being slightly lowered is the sign of relaxation;
neither lowering nor tilting it upward is the sign of bodily balance.
As for the contemplative understanding:
The Sūtra says:
"To suddenly arouse diligence while one’s body is already fully perfected in the six pāramitās is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva."
This body has the characteristic of urgency;
that it does not suddenly arise is also the work of Māra.
This body has the characteristic of expansiveness.
This is neither too hurried nor too relaxed;
it is the characteristic of the body being well-adjusted.
Regarding the fourth, the regulation of breath:
When sitting, if the inhalation and exhalation are too rapid, this is the sign of slickness (*snigdha*).
If the exhalation is congested and obstructed, this is the sign of roughness (*paruṣa*).
If the breath is neither rough nor slick, this is the sign of harmony (*samāhita*).
Regarding contemplative understanding,
the Sūtra says:
"One takes the wisdom of prajñā as one's life-force."
This is tranquility (*śamatha*).
Now, when the wisdom of *prajñā* is neither sharp nor dull,
this is the characteristic of tranquility and meditative cultivation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
When the mind is being tamed, if it frequently pursues objects of perception, this is the sign of agitation;
if it is frequently obscured by darkness, this is the sign of laxity;
when it is neither lax nor agitated, this is the sign that the mind has been tamed.
Regarding "understanding through contemplation," the Sūtra says:
"The bodhicitta is now provisionally manifested."
This is the sign of floating when generating the bodhicitta with partial emptiness;
this is the sign of sinking when generating the bodhicitta with partial emptiness.
Generating the bodhicitta through the Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional, neither sinking nor floating.
This is the characteristic of a well-trained mind.
This refers to the training of the five matters.
As for the five practices and five dharmas:
It refers to desire, diligence, mindfulness, skillful wisdom, and single-mindedness.
As for "desire," it is the longing and aspiration for signless *prajñā*.
The perfectly wondrous and supreme fruit is like Sadāprarudita seeking Prajñāpāramitā and desiring to see Dharmodgata.
Upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā,
one should fix the mind and resolve upon it, seeking nothing else.
This is what is meant by "diligence."
Just as when Sadāprarudita sought the Prajñāpāramitā,
his body and mind were so diligent that he did not perceive day or night,
nor did he feel any exhaustion.
He does not think of food or drink.
Day and night, he exerts himself with diligence, seeking prajñā without any other aspiration.
As for "thinking":
He thought only of when he might see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata;
he thought only of when he might hear the Prajñāpāramitā;
he thought only of when he might become endowed with the pāramitās.
Without any other thoughts,
the one of skillful wisdom contemplates and knows how to relinquish this impermanent and decaying body.
One seeks the adamantine body of the Tathāgata;
one discards impermanent life to seek the prajñā of the eternally abiding life of wisdom.
Having reflected that one not only escapes from this body of great suffering,
but actually obtains the treasure of unsurpassed great benefit.
Even if he were to endure exhaustion and suffering for the rest of his life, he would not perceive it as toil.
Thus, he did not think of fatigue nor of food and drink;
he thought only of when he might succeed in selling his body.
By making offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, one obtains the hearing of the Prajñāpāramitā.
As for "single-mindedness," it means maintaining only the mind of the Middle Way and the true mark of Prajñā.
Furthermore, there is no mind of dual extremes;
this is called "single-mindedness.
Up to this point, the two explanations regarding phenomena and principle have been briefly elucidated.
The explanation of the twenty-five expedient means is concluded.
Although the meaning of these expedient means is not particularly profound or obscure,
they constitute the essential method for beginners who study the Way.
As an excellent guide for those returning to the source,
all twenty-five types [of beings] must employ skillful wisdom and single-mindedness;
through these expedient means, they must harmonize the mind to enter the Right Path.
Therefore, the verse says: "Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself, how are the twenty-five skillful means accomplished?"
"To harmonize the mind and enter the Right Path"—
this is precisely what is meant by that.
*Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*, Fascicle Three.
*Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*, Scroll Four, composed by the Sui Dynasty Tiantai Śramaṇa Guǎngdìng.
The treatise states: Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind that arises of itself, how is it that this causal mind gives rise to the ten kinds of objects?
The realms constitute the one mind and the three wisdoms;
this is the sixth single verse.
This clarifies that while the principle of correct contemplation is ultimately real,
various objects arise in a diverse manner;
nevertheless, regarding the four types of samādhi mentioned above:
The twenty-five expedient means (*upāya*) are all preliminary preparations for clearly cultivating correct contemplation (*samyag-vipaśyanā*).
What follows now is the actual method for clearly cultivating perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the mind":
observing the arising of the ten objects is called "the causal mind.
As for the arising of these ten kinds of objective realms:
First, the sphere of the aggregates;
second, the sphere of afflictions;
third, the sphere of illness.
Fourth, the sphere of the deeds of Māra;
fifth, the sphere of the characteristics of karma;
sixth, the sphere of meditative concentration.
7. The objects of various views;
8. The objects of overweening pride;
9. The objects of the two vehicles.
The ten objects of the bodhisattvas.
First, regarding the observation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*):
since all sentient beings are always accompanied by the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*āyatana*), [the bodhisattva observes them].
One must first contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*), and only thereafter contemplate the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Generally speaking, when water flows, it surges forth; likewise, when the objects of the aggregates are contemplated, they strike and trigger the afflictions, causing the three poisons to stir and overflow in an extraordinary manner.
If one does not understand this,
and the practitioner fails to recognize it, they will inevitably become submerged and overwhelmed by it.
Therefore, the second section clarifies the activity of the arising afflictions and explains how to treat them through contemplation.
Next, regarding the observation of the object of the patient:
all sentient beings, by means of the four great poisonous snakes,
constitute a single body.
This illness is constant;
however, there are many kinds of illnesses,
such as those caused by karma.
Either it is a disease caused by the disharmony of the four great elements,
or a disease caused by malevolent spirits,
or a disease contracted due to the mind being unsettled while practicing seated meditation.
Now, observing that the objects of the aggregates, bases, and elements do not manifest,
yet only various illnesses manifest—
if one does not understand this, they will manifest at such times.
If the practitioner does not recognize [the danger],
they will ruin the mind of the three contemplations;
they will destroy the life-preserving bag and lose right mindfulness.
Third, clarifying the realm of illness.
Next, regarding the observation of the realm of karmic characteristics:
all sentient beings possess all manner of wholesome and unwholesome karma from the past.
However, because the waves of the water of sentient beings' minds are not stilled,
karma cannot manifest. Now,
by means of contemplating the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one clarifies the spirit and settles the meditative absorption.
Past karmic actions arise from a tranquil mind;
if one does not understand this,
one will not recognize them at the moment they arise.
This is because it constitutes a destruction.
Fourth, the characteristics of the arousal of karma are clarified.
Next, one contemplates the sphere of demonic activities (*mārakarma*).
The Sūtra says:
"When the Bodhisattva path is perfected,
one shall transform and guide sentient beings to vacate my palace."
When one's Way has not yet been perfected, one must break through [obstacles];
thus it is said:
"When the Way is lofty, demonic forces flourish."
Now, observe that the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) frequently give rise to demons;
if one does not clarify this beforehand,
the practitioner will not recognize them when they arise.
This is because one is thereby deluded by them.
Fifth is the clarification of the objective realm of demonic activities (*māra-karman*).
Next is the contemplation of the objective realm of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
The Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings have three kinds of fixed dispositions, namely:
superior, middling, and inferior."
The inferior refers to concentration among the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-dharma*).
The middling refers to...
All sentient beings possess the *āsvādana-dhyāna* (tasting-meditation) of the first stage.
As for the superior concentration,
all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Therefore, when one now contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*) and enters the realm of tranquility, many meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) arise.
If these are not clearly understood,
the practitioner will fail to recognize them at the time they arise.
This is because it is that which is to be refuted.
Sixth, the meditative state of dhyāna is clarified.
Next, regarding the observation of the objects of various views:
All sentient beings constantly dwell within the net of various views.
Now, when observing the entry into the aggregates and sense bases,
they produce many views through various forms of conceptualization and analysis.
If one does not understand this,
then at the time of its arising, one will fail to recognize it;
consequently, it will be destroyed by various views.
The seventh clarifies the objects of the various views.
Next, regarding the observation of the object of overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
one now observes the entry into the aggregates (*skandha*) and the sense-bases (*dhātu*).
Or, upon giving rise to even a slight degree [of realization],
they immediately claim to be noble ones;
having not attained what they have not attained, they claim to have realized it and thus fall into overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
If one does not understand this,
one will fail to recognize it when it arises and will consequently become submerged in it; thus,
the eighth [section] clarifies the object of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Next, regarding the observation of the realm of the Two Vehicles,
the Sūtra says:
"I see sentient beings along the Ganges River who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta."
Those who achieve realization are few, while most fall to the stages of the two vehicles.
Now, the practitioner first contemplates the entry into the aggregates and realms,
giving rise to the bodhicitta and training in the path of the bodhisattva.
However, the path of a bodhisattva is difficult to accomplish;
many fall back and give rise to the mind of the two vehicles.
If one does not clarify this,
then at the time of its arising, one will fail to recognize it and thereby destroy the bodhisattva path; thus,
the ninth [section] clarifies the realm of the two vehicles.
Next, regarding the observation of the bodhisattva’s objects:
there are four types of bodhisattvas.
