Now, this view is refuted by again applying the three provisional designations (trividha-prajñapti) and the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi). Why is this?
Just as the arising of a single thought-moment must depend on the objective field of dharmas (dharmadhātu) within emptiness,
this is what is called "conceptual designation based on causes" (hetusamutthāna-prajñapti).
It arises through the continuous succession of the perception of emptiness.
This is the conventional designation of continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*).
When the view of emptiness arises in dependence upon the view of non-emptiness, this is the conventional designation of mutual dependence (*apekṣā-prajñapti*).
Now, I ask: does the cognition of the view of emptiness arise from the mind?
Does it arise from the internal mind?
Does it arise from external empty objects, the dharmas as sensory fields?
Or does it arise from the combination of both the internal and the external?
This is for the purpose of abandoning [the notions of] internal and external arising. If the mind arises internally, it is self-arising;
if external dharmas and sense objects arise, they are other-arising.
If [the object] arises through the conjunction of the internal and external, it would be produced by both;
if it arises apart from the internal mind and external objective fields, it would be produced without a cause.
All four positions entail these faults, as previously refuted.
For those who have not yet resolved this matter regarding the mind, we shall further analyze it in terms of the conventional designation of continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*).
What is meant by this? If one claims that the single moment of empty mind arises from a preceding mind that has not ceased, then it would follow that the mind arises from itself;
or else, the preceding mind must cease before it arises.
This is precisely arising from another;
the preceding mind both ceases and does not cease as it arises.
This is precisely arising from both.
If the preceding mind arises neither through cessation nor non-cessation,
then it would arise without cause; thus,
none of the four logical alternatives can be established.
The refutation of this matter is as before.
Furthermore, if one maintains that [things] exist through mutual dependence,
that too is now refuted.
If it arises depending on an arising mind,
then it arises by itself;
if it arises depending on a non-arising mind, [then it likewise arises by itself].
If arising from another were dependent, then the mind would arise both as arising and as non-arising;
this is arising from both.
If it were dependent on that which is neither arising nor non-arising, then the mind would arise.
That is, it would arise without cause;
thus, none of the four propositions can be established.
In this way, through the three types of conventional designation and the examination of the four propositions, the view of emptiness itself cannot be apprehended.
Yet he knows for himself that his calculations are fixed upon an empty void; the hundred realms are non-existent,
and even the wondrous Dharma of the sages is but delusion and inversion.
The Sūtra states:
"If one says that sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature,
this is to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
If one says that sentient beings definitely lack the Buddha-nature,
this is likewise a slander against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
therefore, it is known that my reckoning of the mind as being definitely existent or definitely non-existent [is not the case].
They immediately slandered and reviled the Triple Gem;
they repented, reproached themselves, and felt shame while confessing their prior transgressions.
These constitute the eighty-eight afflictions (*āsrava*).
The non-arising of the twelve links of dependent origination and the six corruptions that constitute the origin of suffering is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The path that is able to subdue the origin of suffering is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Next, he further reflects: "If the mind were definitively existent, that would be the view of eternalism;
if the mind were definitively non-existent, that would be the view of nihilism.
Thus, one might reckon that the mind both exists and does not exist."
Immediately, a single grade of concentrated mind arises, profound and still;
there is a perception that is both existent and non-existent, and the mind is clear and pure.
One then takes this to be the cause of the Way.
This view causes the mind to give rise again to the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Through the flow of suffering and its origin, it obstructs the Path itself.
This is then examined and refuted by means of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As can be known from the preceding examples,
since neither existence nor non-existence can be found upon investigation,
one realizes that consciousness itself is the mind that perceives both existence and non-existence— the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Next, one further calculates that the mind is neither existent nor non-existent;
when the arising of suffering and its accumulation are examined by means of the three provisional designations and the four propositions,
they cannot be apprehended.
One then perceives the four truths as the mind that is neither existent nor non-existent.
Next, one further calculates that the mind lies beyond the four propositions and is inexpressible;
because it is inexpressible, [it is thus perceived].
When the mind arises again upon seeing [the object],
one investigates suffering and its origin through the three provisional designations and the four propositions;
yet they are found to be unobtainable.
That is to say, one cannot speak of a mind that perceives suffering,
its origin, the path, or cessation as being singular;
this is outside of such single fourfold propositions.
Beyond the fourfold set of propositions, there is an inexpressible proposition;
it is both complete within the fourfold set and yet inexpressible beyond the fourfold set.
In this manner, one successively raises objections and refutes them through successive examination.
Even when searching for it by breaking it apart—whether horizontally or vertically—it cannot be found.
One then realizes that all such calculations are merely inversions;
one repents, reproaches oneself, and feels shame while confessing prior transgressions.
The subduing of the mind that perceives suffering and its origin is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
The wisdom capable of subduing it is called the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).
Thus, one is able to recognize and perceive the Four Noble Truths within the mind.
He is called a practitioner of the Path.
Within this, there should be five points for discernment.
What are they? First, the old illness is not eliminated, and a new illness arises further.
If one does not attain meditative concentration, the two old ailments of the non-Buddhists are removed but new ailments arise.
If one attains dhyāna, the three old ailments of the non-Buddhists are not removed, yet the new ailments are suppressed;
such a person is one who employs the five expedient means.
Fourth, when old illnesses are not yet eliminated but new illnesses have been extinguished,
this refers to one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna).
Fifth, when both old and new illnesses are eliminated, this refers to an Arhat.
Next, regarding the distinction by way of stages:
since non-Buddhists have already given rise to the new affliction of view-delusions,
they lack the vehicle of the Truth of the Path and are thus unable to transport themselves out of birth and death.
If it is a practitioner of the Tripiṭaka who has suppressed the delusions of the view,
they ride upon the semblance of the Truth of the Path and are conveyed to the five stages of expedient means.
If it is a practitioner of the Shared Teaching who has suppressed the delusions of the view...
If one of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) practitioners advances to the stage of the Ten Faiths,
and if one of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) practitioners advances to the Five Ranks (wupin).
Now, when the practitioner contemplates the mind as it emerges from the realms of the six paths and proceeds to the realm of the two vehicles,
if they sever the delusions of views:
The Tripitaka refers to the true illumination of the patience regarding suffering;
in the general sense, it is the stage of insight (darśana-bhūmi),
and in the specific sense, it is the first dwelling (prathama-vihāra).
"Round" refers to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
Question: Since the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are presented both singly and in combination, why are they all said to be "views"?
Answer: Kāśyapa is one who has attained realization;
yet he still says that prior to this, all were called people of wrong views.
How much more so for those of ordinary sentiment today, who, through mere speculation and calculation, claim it is not a view?
If one says it is not seeing,
then one should now have attained the fruit of sainthood;
if one has not yet attained it but claims to have done so, this is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Such a person is not yet fit to discuss the Way.
If one were to discuss it by feeling one's own heart,
before the mind has attained the Way, even if there were a thousand layers and ten thousand folds of words— utterances beyond description and hundreds of phrases— it would all be in vain.
How can it not be a view? For example,
when Dīrghanakha contemplated all phenomena for a long time without finding even a single dharma that entered his mind,
he challenged the Buddha, saying:
If all phenomena are not accepted, does this not then confuse [this teaching] with the Mahāyāna "Samādhi of Non-acceptance"?
Even one of sharp faculties such as Dīrghanakha could not recognize the mind of views regarding suffering and its origin.
How much less could those who are now ordinary and shallow possibly recognize it?
Second, regarding the destruction of the delusions of conceptual thought through the provisional: the delusions of conceptual thought are divided into two categories.
First, clarifying the faults of the afflictions of thought;
second, clarifying the contemplation of dharmas.
Regarding the afflictions of thought:
In the desire realm, there are greed, hatred, delusion, and pride;
in the two upper realms, hatred is excluded from each of these three.
Thus, there are ten afflictions across the three realms in total.
In the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), there are nine grades of volitional afflictions (cetanā).
In the form and formless realms, each of the eight dhyānas and one dhyāna likewise has nine grades.
Thus, there are eighty-one grades of afflictions of volition across the nine stages of the three realms (tridhātu).
Because it is severed through profound reflection, it is called "contemplation" (cintā).
Yet even those who have attained the three fruits are deluded by it;
how much more so the case for ordinary worldlings?
The Sūtra says:
"If one is greedy for wealth and sensual pleasures, one will not attain the Way while sitting [in meditation].
It further says:
A single thought of anger obstructs the gate of illumination of the thousand dharmas.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"From delusion and craving, my illness arises."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"My present illness arises entirely from the delusions and various afflictions of past lives;
it has greed, craving, and ignorance as its root."
Due to ignorance, there arise volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death;
thus do the twelve links of dependent origination circulate,
and the six realms of existence are falsely entangled in poisonous suffering.
The five causes constitute the truth of origination (samudaya-satya),
and the seven effects constitute the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya).
In this way, from the twelve links of dependent origination, the three paths emerge.
The four inversions, the eight sufferings, the six corruptions, and the eighty-four thousand [afflictions] all arise from the three poisons.
The three poisons and ten latent tendencies moisten the three karmas,
universally producing the ten evil deeds and manifold grave offenses.
These afflictions of thought then obscure and obstruct the practitioner;
by what means could contemplation of principle (li-guan) possibly arise?
Therefore, they must be destroyed.
Yet all these are delusions of forgetfulness;
all take ignorance as their root.
There is no taking birth that does not have ignorance as its beginning.
These are the delusions of the five stages outside the realms,
with ignorance as their root.
As the Sūtra says:
The essence of ignorance is fundamentally non-existent;
it exists only through the conjunction of deluded thoughts and causal conditions.
Thus, the root of ignorance is empty and unreal.
How much more so for all delusions—how could they not be empty?
How could the retributive fruits of the three realms possibly be real?
Thus, the source of ignorance is fundamentally unborn from the beginning.
Furthermore, there is nothing in the present that can be extinguished;
for its original nature is pure, and birth-and-death is itself nirvana.
By what cause could delusive confusion arise, and what would there be to extinguish?
If false attachments have not yet ceased, we shall now further examine and refute them by means of the three provisional designations and the four propositions. Why?
Because the opponent says:
How can you say that what is clearly perceived by the world does not exist?
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
"How can one place trust in what is seen by the eyes of cattle and sheep such as yourself?"
Is it then said that [the mind] exists?
Why must one employ the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) to analyze and refute this?
For the arising of the mind depends upon the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya).
This is the provisional designation of causal formation (*hetu-saṃvṛti*).
The arising of a greedy mind in continuous succession from moment to moment is the provisional designation of continuity (*santati-saṃvṛti*).
The existence of the present depending upon the non-arising of the future is the provisional designation of mutual dependence (*apekṣā-saṃvṛti*).
Now I ask:
do the afflictions of thought arise from within the mind,
or do they arise from the external six sense-objects?
Does it arise from the conjunction of the internal mind and external objects,
or does it arise apart from the internal mind and external objects?
None of these four alternatives can be established.
If it arises from within, it would be self-arising;
for example, a grain seed would be able to grow without depending on soil and water.
If it arises from external objects, it would be arising from another.
If it were as you say, then water and soil should be able to produce grain even without seeds.
If production arose from the union of the internal and external, then it would be produced by both together.
Upon examining the internal and external above, however, no such production exists.
How could conjunction give rise [to production]?
It would be like joining two grains of sand, both of which lack oil.
If each were to have its own production, then there would be two productions upon conjunction.
If arising were devoid of both internal and external factors, it would be causeless arising.
Since even arising with a cause cannot be found,
how much less so can there be causeless arising?
Thus, none of the four positions can be established. Nevertheless,
although the causal formation of the conventional has been refuted,
the mind still conceives that it arises through a continuous succession.
Now I ask:
does the preceding mind arise after having ceased, or does it arise without having ceased,
or does it arise both having ceased and not having ceased?
It arises neither through extinction nor through non-extinction.
If a subsequent mind of greed were to arise without the preceding mind having extinguished,
it would entail a logical fallacy of its own arising spontaneously.
If the subsequent craving-mind arises when the preceding mind has ceased,
then there is the fault of arising from another.
If the subsequent craving-mind arises while [the preceding mind] both ceases and does not cease, [then...]
In either case, a logical fallacy arises.
If the preceding mind neither ceases nor does not cease when the subsequent mind of greed arises,
then there is the fallacy of arising without a cause.
The faults of the four propositions may be understood by analogy with what preceded;
thus, when one thoroughly investigates through these four propositions, the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot be found.
Nevertheless, although the continuity [of the afflictions] is thus refuted, [the question remains:]...
Yet you still maintain that the mind arises in dependence upon conditions.
Now I ask:
do you mean that the arising of the mind depends [on conditions]?
Does it arise dependent on a mind that is unborn?
Does it arise dependent on a mind that is both born and unborn?
Or does it arise dependent on a mind that is neither born nor unborn?
If the mind arises depending on an arising mind,
it would arise from itself;
if the mind arises depending on a non-arising mind, [it would likewise be untenable].
If it arises from another,
that is "other-arising. If it arises depending on both [self and other], yet there is no arising, and mind arises,
that is "co-arising."
If the mind were to arise depending on that which is neither arising nor non-arising,
it would then be produced without a cause;
the faults of these four alternatives are to be understood as in the preceding examples.
Thus, when examined through the fourfold analysis of dependent designation,
it too is ultimately empty and non-existent.
In this way, when sought through the fourfold analysis of the three types of designation, the mind cannot be found.
One immediately awakens to the emptiness of the mind and no longer gives rise to grasping or conceptualization.
One realizes that the six sensory objects—forms, sounds, and so forth—do not truly exist as substantial entities.
When the afflictions of thought are suppressed, this is termed the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The wisdom capable of subduing the afflictions is called the Truth of the Path.
Because suffering and its accumulation are extinguished, ignorance is extinguished.
Up to the cessation of old age and death through the cessation of their causal conditions,
the three paths, the six corruptions, the four inversions, and the eight sufferings are all extinguished.
Because the six corruptions are extinguished, one obtains the ox-cart.
Because suffering, its origin, and its cessation are extinguished, one obtains the sheep cart.
Because the twelve links of dependent origination are extinguished, one obtains the deer cart.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
For the śrāvakas, he taught the Four Noble Truths;
for the pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and for the bodhisattvas, he taught the Six Pāramitās.
Riding upon these three vehicles, one leaves the house of the five aggregates and extinguishes the fires of the four inversions and eight sufferings;
this is called "leaving the burning house."
He immediately entered the city of transformation,
attaining all-knowledge,
which is the true dharma-gate of all phenomena.
This is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional.
Regarding the stages,
this corresponds to the stage of the Arhat in the Tripiṭaka [Teaching].
The general [classification] refers to the stage of "having already accomplished" (kṛtāvī-bhūmi);
the specific refers to the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra);
and the perfect refers to the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā).
Regarding the contemplation of the mind, this refers to entering the realm of the Two Vehicles from the realms of the six paths of existence.
Second, as for the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the provisional,
the Sūtra says:
As long as you have not yet perfected the Buddha-dharma, you should not extinguish sensation to attain realization.
Even if your body experiences suffering,
you should contemplate all sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering.
"Since I have been tamed, I must likewise tame all sentient beings.
This clarifies the intention for emerging into the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).
However, there are five intentions for emerging into the conventional realm.
First, with a heart of compassion, one prioritizes others before oneself.
Second, one recollects one's original vow:
at the time of first generating the bodhicitta, one vowed to uproot all suffering for all beings and bestow all happiness upon them.
Having entered emptiness from the conventional,
one has already extracted oneself from the suffering of the four abodes;
now, emerging from emptiness into the conventional, one should appropriately extract sentient beings from their suffering.
Third, although their wisdom is sharp and keen,
they recognize the fault of dwelling in emptiness while abandoning sentient beings; thus,
they are unable to purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, they have not yet fully mastered the teachings of the Buddha-dharma.
Fourth, they possess skillful means;
thus, although they enter into conventional designations, they are not defiled by the six sense objects.
Fifth is the courageous mind of diligence;
it is the courage within the mind regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
This now accords with the five meanings found in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. The intent is the same.
The Sūtra says:
"To take one's own illness as a means to have compassion for the illnesses of others is identical to [the practice of] loving-kindness and compassion."
One should recognize the countless billions of sufferings of past lives;
is this not the recollection of one's original vows?
One should keep in mind the benefit of all sentient beings.
Is it not the case that the fault of knowing through wisdom that one abides in emptiness while failing to benefit sentient beings is the same?
To be mindful of pure livelihood is likewise the same as skillful means.
"Constantly arousing diligence is itself identical to diligence.
This is the sutra clarifying the five meanings;
it is identical to these five intentions.
However, because the followers of the Two Vehicles lack these five matters,
they are unable to emerge into the provisional.
There are precisely three matters for emerging into the provisional.
First, knowing the illness;
second, identifying the medicine;
third, administering the medicine.

First, knowing the illness means knowing the various illnesses of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*)— both mundane and supramundane— that afflict sentient beings.
As the Sūtra says:
Suffering has immeasurable characteristics;
I have not expounded them at all in that sutra,
for they are beyond the capacity of śrāvakas to comprehend.
The truth of origination is likewise so;
because one thoroughly knows this immeasurable origination of suffering,
it is called "knowing the disease."
Second, regarding the medicine of consciousness:
it is like a great physician who is skillfully able to thoroughly understand the various medicines for all the diverse ailments of sentient beings.
Nor is it the knowledge of a single medicine;
rather, it is the knowledge of the various medicines that extinguish both worldly and world-transcending paths.
It is the universal study of the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Sūtra says:
"The Way has immeasurable characteristics;
I have not fully explained them in that sūtra."
This is not known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
cessation is likewise so.
The bodhisattva universally studies this immeasurable dharma-gate of the path and cessation.
Therefore, it is said that one must recognize the medicine.
Third, as for "administering medicine according to the illness," the Sūtra says:
Śāriputra taught the son of a goldsmith to practice the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā),
and he taught the son of a washerman to practice the meditation on counting the breath (ānāpāna-smṛti).
Neither of them realized the Way;
not only did they fail to realize it, but their false views were further increased.
This was the error of failing to understand how to administer medicine according to the illness.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained enlightenment;
this is the manner of administering medicine according to the ailment.
Now, the Bodhisattva is likewise.
Studying this is the method of administering medicine according to the disease;
one bestows the medicinal Dharma in accordance with what the recipient can bear and what is appropriate for them,
ensuring there is no error regarding their capacity.
It is for these three purposes that one emerges from the provisional (samvṛti).
Previously, one entered emptiness from the provisional and universally destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa);
the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) illuminating the truth is called the universal destruction of dharmas.
Now, entering from emptiness into the provisional, one universally studies the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
thereby shattering the dust-like ignorance; thus,
the Dharma-eye illuminates the conventional world.
Administering medicine according to the illness without the error of missing the patient's capacity is called "pervasive penetration of the Dharma.
*Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*, Scroll Four.
Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind, Scroll Five, composed by the Sui Dynasty Tiantai monk Guanding. Part Three:
Explaining the Universal Penetration of the Dharma through the Middle Way Contemplation. This also clarifies five points. What are they?
First is the study of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).
First, one enters emptiness from the conventional to break through compassion based on sentient beings;
next, one emerges from emptiness into the conventional to break through compassion based on phenomena (*dharma-ālambana-maitrī*).
Because one now cultivates the compassion that transcends the two extremes through the Middle Way,
it is called "unconditioned compassion" (anālambana-maitrī).
As the Sūtra says:
That which takes the Tathāgata as its object is called "objectless.
It is of one essence with true reality; being objectless, it universally pervades the Dharma-realm.
Because it uproots suffering and bestows happiness,
it is called "unconditioned compassion of the same essence.
Second, fulfilling one's original great vows:
The Sūtra says:
"I originally made a vow to cause all sentient beings to attain the Way of the Buddha."
Third, it is to seek the Buddha’s wisdom and the Buddha-eye, both horizontally and vertically,
to achieve ultimate awakening and exhaustively fathom the source and its full extent.
Fourth, it is to study great skillful means and uncalculated, excellent expedients.
Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one manifests various transformations.
Fifth is the cultivation of the power of great diligence.
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
Just as there may be one who is brave and capable of performing difficult feats,
seeking the jewel atop the king’s head—
when such a thing occurs, one cultivates the third contemplation.
This contemplation correctly destroys ignorance.
However, since ignorance has no perceptible characteristics,
how can it be contemplated?
Now, if we turn back to examine the wisdom of the preceding two contemplations:
from the perspective of what precedes them, these two contemplations are wisdom;
yet from the perspective of what follows, they become obstacles to wisdom.
Question: Why is it called the "obstruction of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
Answer: The wisdom of the Middle Way is harmonious and non-dual;
because the former two types of wisdom have not yet attained such unification, it is so named.
This is called the fusion of the cognitive hindrances.
First, it is empty yet always provisional;
provisional yet always empty.
Where there is stillness, there has never been anything that does not illuminate;
where there is illumination, there has never been anything that is not still.
Thus, emptiness and the provisional, stillness and illumination, move together as a non-dual unity.
This is precisely the Middle Way: non-dual yet dual, which is to say, moving in tandem.
Thus, although the names of the three contemplations differ, their essence is identical;
though identical, they have never been one.
Although they differ, they have never been three;
though not three, they are called the Three Virtues (triguṇa).
Though not one, it is called by the single name Great Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The three virtues constitute one nirvāṇa; it is neither three nor one.
It is neither vertical nor horizontal, and is inconceivable."
This is the wisdom of the three contemplations, perfectly integrated and profoundly subtle;
wherein neither marks nor marklessness can be apprehended.
This is termed the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation.
Therefore, this refutes the preceding two types of wisdom that lack mutual integration.
Now, I shall precisely clarify the three contemplations in their successive order.
How is it that they are perfectly integrated and non-dual?
If this is so, how does it differ from the Perfect Contemplation?
Answer: If one enters the Middle Way through the three successive contemplations, they are no different from the Perfect [Contemplation].
Therefore, it is described in this way.
Now, let us further examine and refute [this position] by means of three dharmas.
What are they? First, the contemplation of ignorance;
second, the contemplation of the dharma-nature.
Third, contemplating the true conditions.
First, contemplating ignorance:
one contemplates that the preceding two types of wisdom constitute the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is precisely ignorance.
Now I ask:
from what does this cognitive obscuration arise?
If it is claimed that [ignorance] arises from ignorance itself,
this entails the fallacy of self-arising;
furthermore, since ignorance lacks substantial reality, how could it give rise to anything?
If it is claimed that [the effect] arises from the dharmatā,
then it would be "produced by another";
furthermore, the dharmatā itself is without arising.
How can it arise? If one says that it arises through the conjunction with the dharma-nature of ignorance,
then it is co-arising.
If they were separate, they would arise without a cause;
thus, none of the four alternatives can be used as an analogy for the previous refutation.
Second, the refutation by means of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Previously, it was examined that ignorance (avidyā) is unattainable;
yet it was still asserted that ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Now, I ask:
Does it arise from the nature of phenomena that is subject to the cessation of ignorance?
Does it arise from the nature of phenomena that is not subject to cessation?
Or does it arise from the nature of phenomena that is both subject to cessation and not subject to cessation?
It does not arise from a nature that is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished;
all four propositions are untenable.
Third, the refutation by means of the true and the conditional:
Does this ignorance arise from cultivation based on conditions,
or does it arise from cultivation based on the ultimate reality, or is it produced by both causes and conditions together, or without cause?
If it arises from cultivation based on conditions:
One contemplates impermanence through cultivation.
How can it be produced? If it is produced through genuine cultivation, how is that genuine [cultivation] produced?
Both [theories of] co-arising and causelessness are untenable;
these two interpretations differ.
One states that through the cultivation of conditions, reality is revealed.
The second [position] states: "If the cultivation of conditions manifests the true [nature], then that manifestation is self-arising.
If the cultivation of conditions manifests the true [nature] through the cultivation itself, then that cultivation is other-arising."
None of the four propositions are tenable;
they are all refuted as previously demonstrated.
This concludes, in brief, the vertical refutation of the pervasiveness of dharmas through the three sequential contemplations.
The rest is explained in detail as discussed in the *Zhi Guan* (Calming and Contemplation).
Second, regarding the clarification of the non-vertical refutation:
the Round Teaching (*yuanmen*) has already been explained above.
Now, to further present this in brief:
it clarifies the contemplation of the perfect mind.
The ten realms and the six paths constitute the gate of existence (yǒumén).
The phrase "arising and arising" is the gate of emptiness for the two vehicles;
the phrase "arising and non-arising" is the gate of both emptiness and existence for the bodhisattvas.
This is the phrase of "non-arising arising," which is the Buddha-realm; it is neither the gate of emptiness nor the gate of existence.
It is the phrase of "non-arising non-arising.
Now, having observed that a single thought-moment is perfectly endowed with the ten realms.
Is it not the case that one realm is precisely ten realms,
one phrase is precisely four phrases,
and one gate is precisely four gates?
Is it called the "Perfect Gate" (yuanmen)?
Now, regarding those who cultivate contemplation according to this Perfect Gate:
since the gate is universally penetrating, the contemplation is likewise perfectly integrated.

The Perfect Contemplation enters the Perfect Gate. Why is this? When one now contemplates the six realms of existence with a perfect mind, and considers that these realms, in terms of the phenomena of birth, are fully endowed with the ten realms, then the provisional is never not empty and never not middle.
This is precisely the complete subduing of the delusions of the five abodes.
Regarding the observation that the realm of the two vehicles within the mind itself possesses all ten realms:
this is the contemplation of emptiness.
Emptiness has never failed to rely upon the non-central;
it perfectly subdues the five abodes of ignorance.
When contemplating the mind, the Buddha-realm is complete with the ten realms.
In contemplating emptiness, one never fails to contemplate the non-fictitious,
yet always illuminates both simultaneously.
Furthermore, in contemplating the fictitious, one never fails to contemplate emptiness and the middle, yet always illuminates all three simultaneously.
This is provisional;
it is neither characterized by existence nor non-existence,
and thus represents the perfect subduing of the five stages of delusion.
One contemplates emptiness yet never departs from the provisional or the middle;
this emptiness is neither signless nor characterized by signs.
It is the perfect subduing of the five stages of dwelling within contemplation, wherein one never departs from emptiness or the provisional.
This is to traverse both the characterized and the uncharacterized simultaneously;
yet, while traversing them together, one never truly encounters the characterized or the uncharacterized.
This is the state where the single is provisional and all are provisional.
When one is empty, all are empty;
when one is central, all are central;
yet it is neither one nor all.

Question: If emptiness refutes the provisional and the provisional refutes emptiness, such that both emptiness and the provisional are simultaneously refuted, how can they function as a single essence?
Answer: In the world, the four great elements are mutually obstructive and mutually refute one another.
And yet they mutually constitute a single integrated body;
how much more so when the three contemplations of numinous wisdom mutually negate and support one another to achieve the three virtues of the Great Nirvana.
Why should this give rise to doubt?
For when emptiness refutes the provisional, the provisional has no marks;
when the provisional refutes emptiness, emptiness has no marks.
The Middle refutes the errors of the two extremes of emptiness and the conventional;
by employing both, it refutes the Middle itself, thereby not losing the dual illumination of withering and flourishing.
Emptiness supports the conventional, so that through skillful means there is wisdom and liberation.
When relying on the provisional, one possesses the wisdom of emptiness and the understanding of skillful means;
when relying on the middle, both the wisdoms of emptiness and the provisional are quiescent.
Relying on emptiness and the provisional, the middle is constantly employed in tandem with them.
The two birds fly together.
To provide another analogy now:
ice is likened to the provisional.
Water is likened to space,
and moisture is illustrated by its internal nature.
Thus, although the three names— ice, water, and moisture— are distinct, they do not obstruct their identity as one essence.
Although the names of the three contemplations differ, what prevents their essence from being identical?
Thus, when one is negated, all are negated, so that no delusion remains unexhausted;
when one is supported, all are supported, so that no dharma fails to be perfected.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the ten realms within the mind as a totality:
the Buddha-realm is the virtue of the Dharma-body,
and it is also the Tathāgata’s robe.
The realm of the two vehicles is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
This is the virtue of *prajñā*,
and it is also the seat of the Tathāgata.
The realm of the bodhisattva is itself the virtue of liberation;
it is also the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Thus, these three virtues constitute the attainment of great nirvāṇa.
This is called the Practice of Peaceful Abiding.
The three—the Tathāgata’s robe, seat, and chamber—constitute the perfect practice of the Tathāgata;
for this practice is the practice of Nirvāṇa.
This is called "Peaceful Conduct.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata."
This is what is meant by that.
Therefore, one who knows how to universally contemplate the ten realms within the mind is,
in fact, constantly contemplating nirvana while practicing the Path.
To practice the conduct of a Tathāgata is the Practice of Peaceful Abiding. Furthermore,
the three virtues are identical to the three types of *prajñā* and the three types of *nirvāṇa*.
This continues up to the ten kinds of threefold dharmas, which are fully realized within the contemplation of the ten dharma realms.
Furthermore, "peaceful bliss" (anraku) is the oneness of principle,
while "practice" (gyō) is the oneness of practice.
The practitioner is the unity of person;
the teaching of perfect contemplation is the unity of doctrine.
This principle of the fourfold unity is the profound essence of the Lotus Sūtra.
Because it completely shatters the nine dharma-realms,
it is called the "pervasive shattering of dharmas that is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of what is permeable and what is obstructed:
The Lotus Sutra says:
There was a guide who well knew the passages and obstructions,
leading a multitude of people.
Desiring to traverse a perilous path to reach a place of precious treasures,
Vimalakīrti said:
"The various afflictions of my disciples are transformed according to their will."
That is to say:
the practitioner is well able to guide the sentient beings of the mental factors across the perilous path.
The Sūtra says:
"It is better to take the mind as one's teacher than to take the mind as one's master.
Now, observe that the ten realms of the mind are the three contemplations of tranquil illumination.
He guides all mental factors away from the obstacles of the two vehicles;
thus he is the teacher of the mind,
called the Great Guide who well understands what is passable and what is obstructed.
What is it? Within the consciousness-mind, the realms of the six destinies are suffering and its origin;
these obstruct the True Truth.
Within the consciousness-mind, the realms of the two vehicles are the path and cessation.
Although it penetrates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it obstructs the bodhisattva’s conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
although it penetrates the conventional truth within the consciousness-mind, it obstructs the bodhisattva-realm.
Yet it blocks the Middle Way and the First Noble Truth;
within the mind, the Buddha-realm pervades all three truths.
This is merely a discussion of the sequence of what is permeable and what is obstructed.
If the nine realms within the mind of consciousness are themselves the Buddha-realm,
then all obstructions are permeable.
If one is deluded and takes the Buddha-realm within the mind to be the nine realms, [then all is obstructed].
All passages are obstructed.
In the single path of perfect contemplation, which is pure and serene, there is neither passage nor obstruction;
yet passage and obstruction do not hinder one another.
Furthermore, if one contemplates that the mind is merely provisional and not empty,
one immediately increases one's slander;
if one obstructs this contemplation by holding that the mind is empty and not provisional, [one likewise errs].
If one illuminates both emptiness and the conventional without a middle way,
this constitutes the obstruction of increase, decrease, and slander.
To hold merely to the middle while failing to see it as empty and provisional is to be neither existent nor non-existent;
this is called the obstruction of the discourse of the deluded.
If one contemplates the mind as empty yet always provisionally possessing wisdom, there is the understanding of skillful means;
this is penetration, not obstruction.
If one contemplates the mind as provisional yet always empty, there is the understanding of wisdom through skillful means.
This is penetration, not obstruction.
Contemplating that the mind is empty and provisional while remaining eternally in the Middle, such that the two wisdoms are simultaneously quiescent—
this is penetration, not obstruction.
Observing within the mind, one constantly employs both the provisional and the empty, with stillness and illumination acting in tandem;
this is penetration, not obstruction.
Question: Why do you explain both penetration and obstruction by means of the mind?

Answer: As for those who contemplate the mind above but do not attain awakening, it is because they fail to recognize the obstructions and difficulties regarding what is permeable and obstructed, what is deviant and correct within the mind.
All dharma-gates, including even the ten chapters, are discussed in terms of the mind; how could this apply to the single chapter on "Permeability and Obstruction" alone?
To rely on other [commentaries] would be superficial;
for the student to seek it elsewhere would not accord with the intent of this treatise.
Sixth, regarding the harmonization of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*):
there are four types of these factors.
The first is the analytical classification of the factors of enlightenment.
As with the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts,
and so forth, each enters the path from its own respective point.
Second, regarding the inclusion of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma):
This is like the way the six perfections are mutually inclusive.
Third, regarding the stages, it is like the stages from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
This refers to the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
While the four aspects give rise to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
here we are specifically clarifying the path-factors that arise through their mutual conditioning and harmonious integration.
Question: The "Chapter on the Path" (Mārgavarga) belongs to the Dharma of the Two Vehicles;
how, then, does a bodhisattva contemplate it?
Answer: The *Śāstra* (Treatise) explicitly refutes this interpretation.
Who makes this statement?
A sutra says:
"The factors of enlightenment and virtuous friends are that by which one achieves perfect awakening."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path enables one to see the Buddha-nature.
How could this not be the Mahayana?
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
one contemplates that within a single moment of mind there are ten realms and a hundred suchnesses.
Now, observing the mind, one sees that the six destinies and the five aggregates are immediately empty.
The realm of the two vehicles is called the four "withered" applications of mindfulness;
it is the contemplation that the six realms and five aggregates of the mind are merely provisional.
The realm of the bodhisattva is called the four foundations of mindfulness.
To contemplate the mind within the six realms and the five aggregates as being the Buddha-realm is [the practice].
It is neither withering nor flourishing;
it enters the great quiescence of nirvana.
To contemplate that the Buddha-realm is identical to the nine realms is [the realization of the one mind].
This is precisely the simultaneous illumination of both decay and flourishing, where the two birds fly together.
Thus, when contemplating the mind, the ten realms are illuminated yet eternally quiescent;
this is the pair of *śāla* trees within the very heart.
This is the entry into the secret treasury of the three virtues, the Great Nirvana.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvana."
This is precisely the meaning of "no further cessation.
The four foundations of mindfulness were already explained at the beginning of this treatise;
they will not be discussed in detail here.
Furthermore, when observing the realms of the six paths within the mind,
that which constitutes the realm of the two vehicles is precisely the breaking of the demons of the four inversions regarding permanence and bliss.
To contemplate the mind as the realm of the six paths and as the realm of the Bodhisattva is precisely to shatter the demons of the four inversions regarding impermanence.
To contemplate the six elements of the mind as being the Buddha-element is to simultaneously shatter the eight inversions;
it is neither withering nor flourishing, yet it both withers and flourishes.
Second, they move together in stillness while remaining constantly illuminating;
this is precisely to sit at the site of enlightenment within this very mind.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness is what is meant by "sitting at the site of enlightenment.
This is precisely what is being referred to.
Furthermore, the ten realms and hundred suchnesses, when considered within the mind, are called the inconceivable meaning.
Regarding the "quiescence and transcendence of names and marks":
this refers to the mind’s realization of sitting at the site of enlightenment and entering nirvana;
its profound and subtle intent is likewise inconceivable.
Regarding the four right efforts:
one contemplates the ten realms within the mind;
as for the unarisen evil thoughts of the six destinies, one diligently restrains them so that they do not arise.
One exerts effort to abandon and extinguish those [unwholesome states] already arisen;
one exerts effort to give rise to the four noble wholesome minds not yet arisen;
and one exerts effort to cause those already arisen to increase.
These are called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, one diligently exerts oneself to extinguish the nine realms and diligently brings forth the Buddha-realm.
As for the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*):
"Tranquility" (śamatha) is meditative concentration (samādhi).
The previously cultivated foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and right efforts (samyakpradhāna) are all of the nature of wisdom (prajñā).
If wisdom is excessive, there will be distraction;
next, one should cultivate the concentration of supernormal power (ṛddhi-samādhi) to restrain that distraction and bring concentration and wisdom into equilibrium.
This causes one to contemplate and clearly perceive.
As the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings possess three kinds of fixed natures."
That is to say, there are superior,
middling, and inferior.
The inferior refers to concentration of the mental factors (*caitasika*).
The middling refers to the savoring of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The superior refers to...
The Buddha-nature is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
this is the fundamental habit of quiescent concentration possessed by all sentient beings.
Now, by practicing *yathābhūta* (as-it-is), one quiets distraction and returns to this fundamental concentration.
The Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi;
they are the originally present luminosity of wisdom."
Now, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) to cause them to return to their original source, which is purity.
As for the five faculties (pañcendriya),
they are faith, diligence, concentration, wisdom, and mindfulness.
Cultivating the foundations of mindfulness as above,
concentration and wisdom are tranquil and illuminating;
the source of the mind and the hundred suchnesses of the ten realms are clearly understood without doubt.
The faculty of faith arises.
The advancement through right effort is the faculty of energy.
The arising of mindfulness and wisdom and their increasing clarity is the arising of the faculty of wisdom.
The faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) arises when one’s meditative absorption increases as desired.
The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛti-indriya*) arises when concentration and wisdom are balanced.
As for the five powers (*pañca-balāni*):
They are faith, energy, concentration, wisdom,
and mindfulness. As for "powers," faith overcomes the obstacle of doubt.
Vigor overcomes the obstacle of indolence; concentration overcomes the obstacle of distraction; wisdom overcomes the obstacle of delusion;
and mindfulness overcomes the obstacle of wrong views.
Because it can thus overcome these five obstacles.
These are called the five powers (*pañca-balāni*). As for the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*), they are:
joy, energy, discernment, equanimity, concentration, and mindfulness.
Although the superior [practitioner] has, through concentration and wisdom, illuminated the source of the mind,
if they have not yet attained awakening,
there is fear that their sinking and floating will remain inconsistent.
By employing the seven factors of enlightenment to bring about balance, one attains single-mindedness.
As the Sūtra says:
"Governed by single-mindedness, one traverses the Eightfold Noble Path."
Why is this? If the mind is sunken or dull,
one should employ the three factors of enlightenment— discrimination, joy, and energy— to rouse it.
If the mind is floating or distracted,
one should employ the three factors of enlightenment related to relinquishment (*praśrabdhi*) to still the agitation.
If the mind is neither sunken nor floating, [one should maintain equanimity].
One should employ the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness to quiescently illuminate the source of the mind.
Furthermore, if one contemplates the mind as exclusively empty, this is the sign of sinking;
if one contemplates the mind as exclusively provisional, this is the sign of floating.
Rightly contemplating the Middle Way is neither sinking nor floating;
this is called "single-mindedness.
If the seven factors of enlightenment do not enter [into practice], [one has not yet attained it].
One should further cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
Contemplate the mind through the ten realms and the hundred suchnesses as in the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness;
contemplate that the mind is neither withering nor flourishing, yet simultaneously illuminates both withering and flourishing.
To fully possess the three contemplations within a single mind is called right view;
to investigate and reflect upon this principle is called right thought.
To speak to others of the correct contemplation of the mind is called right speech.
This contemplation, which can bring about sublime fruits, is called right action.
This wisdom is called right livelihood.
The Middle Way within a single mind is called right mindfulness;
this contemplation, which can destroy the delusions of the two extremes,
is called right wisdom.
This contemplation, which can arrest the distractions of the two extremes, is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
As for the analogies: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like seeds;
right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is like the sprouting of shoots.
The five faculties are like the roots from which they grow;
the five powers are like the stems and leaves;
and the seven factors of enlightenment are the flowers.
The Eightfold Noble Path is like a fruit.
Thus, a sutra says:
"The flowers of the pure and wondrous awakening-mind yield the fruit of liberation and wisdom."
This is indeed so. However, as one approaches the city of Nirvana through the factors of the path, there are the three gates:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They are also called the three liberations and the three samādhis.
Entering meditative concentration from right view and giving rise to untainted wisdom is called the Great Minister.
Concentration is named the Great King;
therefore, it is said that the three samādhis are not wisdom nor meditation alone.
Right concentration gives rise to right view, and the development of untainted concentration serves as its minister.
Right view is the great king;
it is called the three gates of liberation, for there is neither dhyāna nor wisdom without them.
Within the three baskets, under the category of suffering, the two—emptiness and non-self—are the gate of emptiness.
The extinction of the lower four [truths] constitutes the gate of signlessness (*animitta*).
The eight [truths] of origination and the path, together with the last two of the truths of suffering, totaling ten, constitute the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*), the emptiness of both suffering and its origination constitutes the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, not reckoning the characteristic of emptiness is called the gate of signlessness;
likewise, the absence of one who can contemplate is called the gate of wishlessness.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), entering emptiness from the conventional is the gate of emptiness;
furthermore, being without the mark of emptiness itself is emerging from emptiness into the conventional,
which is called the gate of signlessness.
Since there is neither the characteristic of emptiness nor the characteristic of the provisional,
one enters the Middle Way; yet,
even the characteristic of the Middle Way does not exist.
The aspiration for the name may be termed the "Gate of Non-action.
The three samādhis of the Perfect Teaching constitute its perfect function.
Since one enters through successive stages of destruction, it is appropriate that one enter Nirvana via the Gate of the Three Samādhis of the Separate Teaching.
Seventh, cultivating the six perfections as aids to the Path.
Why is this? Because although one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) above, the true illumination does not open up due to being unbalanced;
the mind is obscured by stinginess and greed, and one clings to and cherishes the body and wealth.
They delude the mind and spirit,
and thus vainly obstruct rational contemplation.
As the Sūtra says:
If one is greedy for wealth and sensual pleasures, one will sit [in meditation] yet fail to attain the Way;
this arises from being unable to relinquish the two types of retribution: the dependent and the primary.
Those who are entangled in the bonds of craving can never awaken to the Way.
For instance, Sadāprarudita gave away his marrow, which is so difficult to give,
and sold his body, which is so difficult to sell.
If one seeks prajñā in this way,
how much more so with material wealth? Thus,
will one not surely fulfill one's vows in the City of Fragrance (Gandhavatī)?
He was one who realized Prajñāpāramitā in the Eastern Land.
Yet, throughout accumulated kalpas, he had repeatedly squandered his body and wealth without ever doing so for the sake of the Way.
Now, he is able to renounce this body that is certain to perish.
If one seeks the Way with total dedication, why worry about not attaining it?
In the world, there are those who, driven by anger and valor, cast away their lives to enter the ranks of battle;
among such as these, those who die number in the billions.
The Sūtra states:
"Those who die by the sword shall surely fall into hell;
what benefit, then, is there [in such death]?"
There are those who practice now who will surely be able,
through their fierce courage and self-sacrifice, to defeat the four Māra kings;
how could they not untie the bright pearl from within their topknots and give it to them?
Alternatively, while correctly practicing contemplation, a mind that violates the precepts may arise;
the three karmas become discordant and one transgresses the monastic discipline,
thereby preventing the contemplation of principle from opening up.
The Sūtra says:
"If śīla (ethical discipline) is not pure, samādhi (concentration) will not manifest.
Therefore, one applies the mind [to purify it].
Taking up the precepts as a bridge and as the feet for crossing the great river of birth and death,
one may then attain deliverance.
Therefore, in order to cross the great ocean of birth and death,
the bodhisattva cherishes even a speck of dust from his life-preserving float and does not discard it;
the practitioner should take this as their model.
Alternatively, when practicing contemplation, if the obscuration of anger arises and one constantly dwells on the nine grounds for resentment to obstruct the rational contemplation,
at that time one should cultivate a mind of patience.
The Sūtra says:
"Patience is the foremost path; Nirvāṇa is what the Buddha calls supreme.
When others approach with crookedness, I respond with straightforwardness."
With a sincere heart free from anger, one is naturally upright in principle.
As the Sūtra says:
"Even when angry, always wear the Tathāgata’s robe."
The robe of the Tathāgata is gentleness and patience.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
If various evils should befall you, you should endure them by recollecting the Buddha;
for if one abides in the holy words, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Alternatively, when practicing contemplation, if laziness arises in the mind, one will be unable to achieve awakening.
One must apply diligent effort.
For even a minor undertaking cannot be accomplished if the mind lacks resolve and determination.
How much more so, then, for one who wishes to clear the heavy barriers of the five stages and cross the great ocean of birth and death—
how could they fail to apply diligent effort?
By what means can one realize the wondrous Way?
It is like Pōlún standing by the roadside,
who for immeasurable time never thought of weariness.
He did not think of day or night;
he did not think of food or drink.
He thought only of when he might see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
It is because of his diligence that he ultimately attained spiritual resonance with the unseen realm;
hence it is said:
"Because all Buddhas are single-mindedly diligent and energetic."
If one can attain *sambodhi*,
how much more so other wholesome dharmas?
This is why the Rishi prostrated before the white bones to express his gratitude for his past diligence.
The hungry ghosts beat their own corpses to repay for their past indolence;
if they do not now strike their own bodies to advance on the Path,
what benefit will it be to harbor weary thoughts later?
At times, while one is correctly practicing contemplation, a distracted mind may arise;
at such a time, one should further cultivate meditative stillness (*śamatha*).
As the Sūtra says:
Sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas,
his body, hands, and feet remain tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving.
How could such a contemplation of principle not cause [the aspiration for awakening] to arise?
The *Śāstra* states:
"When the dust of the world obscures the sun in the sky,
the rain from heaven can submerge it."
The winds of vitarka and vicāra stir the mind;
meditative concentration (dhyāna) can extinguish them.
Dhyāna is like clear, cool water.
It is able to wash away all afflictions;
meditation is a treasury of sharp wisdom and a field of merit for all virtues.
Therefore, one should know that dhyāna possesses various functional capacities;
it is appropriate to apply the mind to its cultivation as an aid to insight meditation (*vipaśyanā*).
Alternatively, when practicing insight meditation properly, a state of mental darkness may arise.
One should cultivate skillful means.
What is the superior cultivation of the perfect contemplation?
It is to contemplate that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
Yet, one does not give rise to fear regarding birth and death,
and instead frequently gives rise to indolence and arrogance; therefore, one should cultivate the contemplations of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self,
and employ the five kinds of impurity as auxiliary practices to spur the mind toward the principle of contemplation.
Why is this so? Although the principle is perfectly pervasive, it has not yet been realized;
how, then, could one immediately be exempt from the fear of impermanence?
This has briefly clarified how the six perfections assist in the development of contemplation of the principle.
If one does not yet attain awakening,
one should further contemplate these six perfections as aids to the path.
This refers to the principle of the inconceivable "Chapter on the Path" (Mārgavarga), which encompasses all dharma-gates through contemplative observation;
it reveals that the power of the six perfections is great enough to destroy delusions by concurrently cultivating both phenomena and principle.
Just as the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is subsumed within the factors of the path in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*),
it abandons the two extremes of birth-and-death.
As the Sūtra says:
Having abandoned both the prior and posterior limits of birth and death,
one becomes free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
attaining the indestructible and eternally abiding state.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be empty;
they are also designated as conventional names."
It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Now, observing the arising and ceasing within the realms of the six paths of rebirth by means of contemplating the mind, and thereby abandoning afflictions—
this is precisely the "dharmas produced by causes and conditions."
The three baskets of the teachings concern the practice of giving through renunciation.
One contemplates that the realm of the two vehicles is itself emptiness,
thereby relinquishing the prior limit of birth and death.
Contemplating the mind as the realm of sentient beings is the provisional [truth],
which abandons the future limit of birth and death.
Contemplating the mind as the realm of Buddhas is the Middle Way.
Thus, one departs from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
attaining indestructible permanence;
this is precisely the practitioner who, with a single mind, performs the perfect contemplation of the ten realms.
This is precisely the complete cultivation of the factors of the path (*mārga-dharma*) across the four teachings, wherein one relinquishes both phenomena and principle through giving (*dāna*).
By completely relinquishing the future limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*),
one attains indestructible permanence.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) in both its phenomenal and principled aspects.
For those who have not yet attained such realization,
they should further cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), specifically right action (samyak-karmānta) and right livelihood (samyag-ājīva).
This is subsumed under the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Previously, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the six perfections were distinguished in relation to the mind;
now, we shall again distinguish the ten kinds of ethical discipline regarding phenomena and principles in relation to the mind.
What is the contemplation of the mind as the realm of the six destinies?
It is the practice of the four precepts, beginning with the precept of maintaining the discipline without deficiency and ending with the precept of being unmixed [with worldly things].
As for the contemplation of the mind as the realm of the Two Vehicles:
This refers to upholding the two precepts of "following the path" and "non-attachment.
Regarding the Bodhisattva realm of contemplating the mind,
this refers to upholding the two precepts of "praised by wisdom" and "sovereignty."
Regarding the contemplation of the mind as the Buddha-realm:
this is precisely upholding the precepts of the "concomitant with meditative concentration" (anuvartaka-śīla).

This constitutes the Middle Way among the three categories of phenomena within the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka)—namely, the causes and conditions, arising and ceasing, and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) pertaining to the six realms of existence.
The precepts of right action and right livelihood consist of contemplating that the mind is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle;
they comprise the middle-way factors of right action and right livelihood within the teachings and principles of the Shared, Distinct, and Complete vehicles.
This is the perfect contemplation of the ten realms as the simultaneous integration of phenomena and principle— that is, the observance of the precepts.
If one has not yet attained awakening,
one should further contemplate the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) among the five faculties within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Among the five powers, it is the power of mindfulness;
among the seven factors of enlightenment, it is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness;
and within the eightfold noble path, it is right mindfulness.
This is precisely what is subsumed under the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Now, following the previous example, we shall again examine the six realms within the mind through contemplation;
this refers to the "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinaya-kṣānti*) regarding the phenomena of dependent origination.
Contemplating the realm of the two vehicles within the mind,
it is immediately emptiness and the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Contemplating the realm of the bodhisattvas within the mind.
This is provisionally termed the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Contemplating the Buddha-realm within the mind is termed the "patience of quiescence" (śānti-kṣānti) within the Middle Way.
These three types of patience constitute the principle.
This is precisely the practice of patience through the complete contemplation of the mind as it fully possesses both principle and phenomena across the ten realms.
For those who have not yet attained awakening:
Furthermore, contemplate the eightfold path of the *mārga*;
observing the realms of the six paths within the mind is the practice of diligence in accordance with reality.
Contemplating the realm of the two vehicles within the mind,
one immediately attains the vigor of emptiness;
contemplating the realm of the bodhisattvas within the mind.
This is because one departs from provisional diligence.
As the sutra says: "One possesses courage regarding the mind within birth and death.
Contemplating the Buddha-realm within the mind is itself the diligence of the Middle Way.
The Sūtra states that all Buddhas attain *sambodhi* through single-minded diligence.
This refers to the perfect contemplation of the mind wherein the ten realms are fully present, embodying both principle and phenomena, as well as diligence.

For those who have not yet attained awakening, one should further consider that the factors of the path (*mārga*), the eight liberations, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of right concentration are all subsumed within the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Contemplating the realms of the six paths within the mind is the cultivation of the four dhyānas and four concentrations among the samādhis of the phenomenal realm.
Contemplating the realms of the two vehicles within the mind is the cultivation of the samādhi of the True Truth through the refinement and permeation of contemplation.
Contemplating the realm of Bodhisattvas within the mind is the cultivation of the samādhi of conventional truth.
Contemplating the realm of Buddhas within the mind is the cultivation of the ninefold Great Dhyāna, the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi.
This constitutes the complete contemplation within the mind, wherein the ten realms fully cultivate both the phenomenal and the principle aspects of all meditations.
For those who have not yet attained awakening, they should further contemplate the ten wisdoms among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*):
the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the two factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation and joy, right view, and right thought.
This wisdom is subsumed within the perfection of prajñā.
If one contemplates the realms of the six destinies within the mind, this is the cultivation of conventional knowledge;
if one contemplates the realms of the two vehicles within the mind, this is the cultivation of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Contemplating the mind as the realm of bodhisattvas is the cultivation of the knowledge of the paths;
contemplating the mind as the realm of buddhas is the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes.
Thus, within the contemplation of the mind, the ten realms fully embody the various pāramitās of both phenomena and principle.

However, the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka primarily apply themselves with diligent effort and arduous perseverance toward the six perfections within the realm of phenomena, and there is nothing superior to this.
The bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) primarily cultivate the six perfections based on the principle of emptiness; therefore, the three [subjective] factors are all extinguished.
Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) mostly employ the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) in their provisional emergence to transform sentient beings.
Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) mostly cultivate the six perfections based on the Middle Way.

Thus, regarding the mutual inclusion, mutual sublation, mutual cultivation, and mutual identity of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) and the six perfections, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and so forth.
How do the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) subdue the sense faculties?
By contemplating that the mind and the realms of the six destinies are phenomena produced by causes and conditions, one thereby employs the six perfections to subdue the sense faculties.
Observing the mind within the realm of the Two Vehicles is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which subdues the sense faculties and brings about detachment from the defilements of the six sense objects.
Observing the mind within the realm of the Bodhisattvas is the provisional (*prajñapti*), which subdues the sense faculties and brings about detachment from the defilement of attachment to emptiness.
Contemplating that the Buddha-realm is identical to the mind is the Middle Way; it subdues the sense faculties and brings one away from the defilements of the two extremes.
With single-mindedness, one performs the perfect contemplation of the ten realms.
The six pāramitās of phenomena and principle are as previously explained.
This refers to the perfect mastery over the sense faculties.
As the Sūtra says: "That which is called the eye-faculty is, with respect to all Tathāgatas, always fully perfected and without diminution;
it perceives with absolute clarity."
Even up to the mental faculty (*manas*), because it is regulated through perfect contemplation,
one may know by subtle inquiry that all five faculties are likewise called "constant."
How are the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) subsumed within the Buddha’s majestic deportment?
The Buddha takes the ten powers (daśabala), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the unique qualities (āveṇikadharma), and so forth, as his majestic deportment.
As for the ten powers:

However, the realms of the six paths are the dharmas born of causes and conditions, which are the four truths of arising and ceasing; within the mind, the realm of the two vehicles is the four truths of non-arising;
and within the mind, the realm of the bodhisattvas is the four immeasurable truths.
The Buddha-realm within the mind is precisely the Four Noble Truths of Non-action.
Now, through the contemplation of tranquil illumination, one realizes that the suffering and accumulation of the six realms within the mind return to those very six realms;
this is indeed possible.
If one were to reach nirvana [through those other paths], such a thing is impossible.
Each [of the Buddhas] clearly perceives these; the same applies to the remaining three sets of the Four Truths regarding suffering and its origin.
This is called the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).
To clearly perceive that the origination of the fourfold Four Noble Truths is the power of karma;
to clearly perceive that the suffering of the fourfold Four Noble Truths is the power of the roots;
the same applies to the path and cessation.
To clearly perceive the eight factors of the path within the fourfold Truth of the Path is the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*).
To know the past suffering and its origin among the sentient beings of the ten realms within one's own mind is the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*).
To know the present suffering and its accumulation among the sentient beings of the ten realms is the power of desire (*chanda-bala*).
To know the future suffering and its accumulation among the sentient beings of the ten realms is the power of nature (*svabhāva-bala*).
To know the fourfold paths is the power of reaching the destination (*prāpti-sthāna-bala*).
To know the four kinds of the truth of cessation is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*).
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*):
one contemplates the ten realms within the mind as the four kinds of the truth of suffering and distinguishes them for others.
Furthermore, it reveals the faults of those sentient beings who are subject to mental afflictions.
It is the definitive lion’s roar, free from even the slightest sign of fear and incapable of being refuted;
this is the fearlessness regarding the knowledge of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Knowing that the four kinds of obstacles to the Truth of Origination are extinguished by the four kinds of paths,
he utters the definitive lion’s roar without the slightest sign of fear;
no one is able to challenge him by saying, "This does not obstruct the path."
This is the fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path.
Knowing the fourfold Truth of the Path and being able to explain how it can exhaust suffering constitutes the fearlessness regarding the path that exhausts suffering.
The fearlessness regarding the teaching that all four truths of cessation have been fully realized is the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).
As for the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*):
Absence of error in body and speech is precept (*śīla*).
Absence of an undisciplined mind is concentration (*samādhi*).
There is no decrease in aspiration, no decrease in vigor, and no decrease in mindfulness.
These are the eight kinds of diligence.
Wisdom does not diminish, liberation does not diminish, and the knowledge and vision of liberation do not diminish.
His three types of action proceed in accordance with wisdom; these are the twelve unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
These are the ten kinds of wisdom.
They, in turn, are fully subsumed within the factors of enlightenment and the six perfections.
As for the four unhindered [knowledges]:
To know that the speech of sentient beings within the ten realms differs within the mind is the unimpededness of language.
To know the fourfold Four Noble Truths is [the unimpededness of phenomena].
This dharma is unimpeded.
To know the meaning of the four kinds of truths is the unimpededness of meaning.
To preach the Four Noble Truths without end is the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
As for the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*):
The three supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) of the divine eye, the divine ear, and the mind-made body are as explained in the section on the "Disciplining of the Faculties.
The [knowledges of] others' minds, past lives, and the destruction of outflows are as explained in the section on the "Ten Powers" (daśabala).
The three types of clear knowledge (vidyā) are as explained in the section on the "Six Supernormal Knowledges."
Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*):
relinquishment is the integration of giving (*dāna*);
right action and right speech are the integration of kind words (*priyavāditā*).
The eight concentrations correspond to the two means of attraction: beneficial conduct and cooperation.
Because concentration gives rise to supernormal powers, one is able to cooperate with others. As for dhāraṇī:
The four right efforts that give rise to the wholesome are the dhāraṇī.
As for the thirty-two marks,
the fourfold path of the truth of the path (mārgasatya) and its constituent factors serve as their cause.
Briefly stated, twelve dharma-gates are sufficient to encompass all auxiliary paths for the six perfections;
how much more so for the true path itself!

Furthermore, the three contemplations and four teachings each possess their own sets of thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas), the six perfections, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all other such dharma-gates.
Now, observing that the mind is replete with the ten realms is itself the three contemplations.
Regarding the four teachings, what teaching, what principle, what practice, what wisdom, what stage, what delusion, or what dharma is there that is not fully encompassed by them?
Therefore, a sutra says: "By breaking the subtle dust of the mind, one brings forth the great thousand-fold world-system sutra scroll.
It further says: "The minds of sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha; there is no dharma not contained therein.

The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings.
